title: What you will be able to do
instruction: Press reveal to see each outcome for this lesson.

_items.text: Treat being critical as a habit of mind you carry into everyday situations, not something you switch on only for assessed work.

title: Being critical, all the time
body: Tutors use the word 'critical' as though everyone already agrees what it means, and they expect you to be critical everywhere, not just in the essay that gets marked. If you only question things when a deadline says you must, the habit never properly forms, and it will not be there when you need it in a seminar, in a job, or simply in deciding what to believe.

title: A mindset, not a mode
body: 'Being critical' is a mindset, a way of thinking and acting that is characteristic of the approach of a successful, self-regulating student to learning (Dennis and Abbott, 2026). That is the whole point: a mindset runs underneath everything you do, while a mode is something you step into and out of. The difference matters because a mode disappears the moment nobody is checking.

definition: A way of thinking that runs by default, without anyone prompting it, rather than a deliberate action you perform only when a task requires it.
extendedDefinition: Being critical becomes a habit of mind when the same questioning applies automatically outside assessment: in a seminar, a job, or everyday reading, not only when a piece of work is being marked.
example: A habit of mind would have you question a claim shared in a group chat the same way you question a source in an essay, without anyone telling you to.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider a claim that a certain revision method 'doubles your grade', shared on social media.

{{learner-a}} finds it interesting, shares it with a friend, and moves on. The claim has been read and passed on, but {{learner-a}} has not asked where the figure came from, what counted as 'doubling', or what was left out. Nothing about the moment prompted the questions, so they go unasked.

{{learner-b}} reads the same claim and pauses on it, the same way she pauses on a claim in a seminar: who produced this figure, what counted as 'doubling', and what is missing. She is not being marked on this. The three questions surface out of habit, in a context nobody set up for her.

Both encountered the same claim. Only {{learner-b}} brought the habit of mind to it, turning a shared post into a question.

title: Why this counts as being critical
body: Nothing about the second version is harsher or more disagreeable than the first. The difference is that it became automatic: the same three questions (where does this come from, what does it actually show, what is missing) now surface without anyone prompting them. That is what turns critical thought into a habit of mind rather than a task you perform for assessment.

instruction: Select a highlighted phrase to read why it matters.

_passage.text: The same three questions turn up throughout this lesson.

_passage._note: This asks you to find the source and its authority, not just accept a claim because it is in front of you.
This checks the claim against the evidence actually offered, rather than the headline version of it.
This asks what the claim leaves out, since an omission can be as misleading as an error.

_passage.text: None of the three is about disagreeableness. All three are about habit.

displayTitle: Three settings where the habit might switch off
instruction: Select each tab to see what switching the habit off looks like there, and what leaving it on would take.

_items.title: Seminar
_items.body: A seminar already asks you to question what's said, but it is easy to let that stop at the door when the group moves to small talk afterwards. Leaving the habit on means still asking where a casual claim comes from, even once the formal discussion has ended.

_items.title: Group chat
_items.body: A share in a group chat rarely comes with a source attached, and nobody there is grading your response. Leaving the habit on means pausing on a claim exactly as you would in a seminar: what is the evidence, and what has been left out.

_items.title: Part-time job
_items.body: At work, a colleague's claim about 'what customers want' can be stated with total confidence and no evidence at all. Leaving the habit on means noticing that confidence is not the same as evidence, in a setting where nobody is marking you on it.

displayTitle: Building the habit, move by move
instruction: Open each move to read it. You can keep more than one open at once.

_items.title: Move 1: Notice the moment
_items.body: Catch yourself about to accept a claim without checking it, wherever that happens.
_items.advice: In practice: the moment is often outside coursework entirely, a social media post, a confident colleague, a line in a seminar discussion.

_items.title: Move 2: Ask the three questions
_items.body: Where does this come from, what does it actually show, and what is missing.
_items.advice: In practice: you do not need all three every time. Even one, asked consistently, starts to form the habit.

_items.title: Move 3: Let it run without being asked
_items.body: Notice when the questioning happens on its own, with nobody prompting it.
_items.advice: In practice: this is the real test. If the questioning only appears when a tutor sets the task, it is still a mode, not yet a habit.

_items.title: Move 4: Carry it into the next setting
_items.body: Take the same questioning into a setting you have not tried it in yet: a job, a club, a different kind of reading.
_items.advice: In practice: the habit is not finished until it has crossed into a setting nobody designed for you.

title: Building the habit outside assessment
body: You do not need a marked task to practise this. The next time you read a claim anywhere, in a lecture, a group chat, or an article, try asking three questions before you accept it: what is the evidence, who benefits if this is believed, and what has been left out. None of this takes long, and the point is not to become suspicious of everything. It is to make questioning the default, so it is already running when an assessed task actually needs it.

title: Decision scenario
body: A classmate states a statistic as settled fact during a seminar discussion, with no source given. Work through the discussion, each choice leads somewhere different.
instruction: Read each situation and choose a response to see what happens next.
ariaRegion: Decision scenario. Read each situation and choose a response to see what happens next.

s1.body: A classmate states a statistic as settled fact during a seminar discussion, with no source given. How do you respond?

_choices.text: Accept it and move the discussion on.
_choices.consequence: The discussion moves faster, but an unchecked claim is now part of the record.

_choices.text: Ask where the figure comes from.
_choices.consequence: A fair, low-key question that keeps the discussion open.
You may be right, but without asking first, the exchange becomes a confrontation rather than a question.

s2.body: Later, you want to reference the same figure in your own essay. What now?

_choices.text: Use it anyway, since it was accepted in the seminar.
_choices.consequence: An unverified claim now carries your own name as well.

_choices.text: Go back and check the original source before using it.
_choices.consequence: Slower, but it is now something you can actually stand behind.

s3.body: You trace the figure to its original source. It roughly holds up, but with caveats the seminar discussion did not mention. How do you use it?

_choices.text: Cite the original source directly, caveats included.
_choices.consequence: The claim now carries a source and its limits, not just a seminar's confidence in it.

_choices.text: Cite it vaguely as 'discussed in a seminar'.
_choices.consequence: Honest, but a specific source would have made the point far stronger.

good.body: The figure checks out, with a proper source and its caveats behind it now. The habit of mind did its work before the claim went any further.

neutral.body: The claim survives, but only loosely sourced. A specific reference would have made the same point far more convincing.

poor.body: An unverified claim ends up in your own work, or the exchange turns into a confrontation instead of a question. Either way, the lesson is the same: ask before you accept or reject.

title: Building the habit outside assessment
body: Use these questions to notice whether the habit is running outside assessment, not just inside it.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it this week.

_items.text: Did I question a claim this week that nobody was marking me on?
Did I ask where a claim came from before I repeated it?
Did I notice a setting where I usually switch the questioning off?
Did I keep questioning something after the formal discussion had ended?
Did I apply the same three questions to something outside my course reading?
Did I carry on asking a question even once I had an easy answer available?

title: Your turn
instruction: This is for your own reflection; no right answers are expected.

_items.text: Think of one moment this week, outside of any coursework, when you questioned something you read, heard or were told. What made you pause?
Is there a setting (a seminar, a part-time job, a group chat) where you tend to switch the questioning off? What would it take to leave it on there too?
